title: The New German Health Minister, A Lawyer, Not A Doctor, Wants To Make It Harder For Elderly Germans to Get Medical Cannabis. Of Course She Wouldn’t Put It That Way

content_html_sanitized:
Nina Warken, the new German Health Minister, wants to ban telemedicine prescriptions for cannabis.

 

She says, “Cannabis is an intoxicating drug and can be particularly harmful to adolescents and young adults. Therefore, I want to restrict the easily accessible online prescriptions."

Now, let me begin by declaring my interest.

First, I am the President of Weed.de, an online service that, among other things, provides access to telemedicine prescriptions for cannabis in Germany and elsewhere in the European Union. 

Second, let me also add that I am almost 85 years old and I have been advocating for easy access to medical cannabis for decades, but now especially for my contemporaries. 

We should be able to do this without having to get a doctor’s appointment, then get on a bus, and then sit in a waiting room with people who may be really sick, and then answer questions that could easily be answered online from a doctor who has no medical training about cannabis. Indeed, the medical profession has largely opposed medical cannabis, and very few of them have any training in medical cannabinoids. 

Plus, no doctor can tell just by looking at me if I really have trouble sleeping, or if my sciatica is really bothering me, or if I am just depressed because I have to please a lawyer who knows even less than the doctor just to get some weed. 

Can I get a prescription for “anger management”?

Meanwhile in the real world, from DW.com March 17, 2024: “Germany is facing an alarming rise in crack cocaine and fentanyl abuse, with nearly 2,000 drug-related deaths reported in 2022. Experts are calling for comprehensive strategies to address the crisis.”

Germany also has a serious problem with prescription benzodiazepines. From Problematic Medication With Benzodiazepines, “Z-drugs”, and Opioid Analgesics “An estimated 1.4 to 2.6 million people in Germany  suffer from drug dependence. Most of them are long-term users of benzodiazepines (BZD), Z drugs (ZD), or opioid analgesics (OA). 

This is something that deserves the Health Minister’s time. See General practitioners’ concepts on issuing out-of-pocket prescriptions for hypnotics and sedatives in Germany

Of course, given the aging of the general population, plus the aging of medical professionals, and the resulting difficulty getting doctor appointments, telemedicine is going to play an increasingly important role in health care. Clearly, doctors have better things to do with their time than encouraging people to go back to the black market.
